Each sibling's agent holds their stated availability and limits, a parent agent holds the parent's own written preferences and has first say on what they accept, and a shared ledger tracks visits, drives and money over months, so fairness is visible instead of argued. Nobody has built it because it needs persistent multi-party agents with real calendar access and consent from everyone, which neither developer tools nor consumer family apps provide.
dossier.demo_60s: A demo family of three siblings and a parent shows a month grid. A new event, 'Mom's cardiology appointment Thursday 2pm', arrives and the agents trade proposals in a side feed. The ledger shifts 'Dana +1 drive, Marcus +1 phone call', the parent's agent vetoes a Sunday slot citing her written note, and a deadlock the agents can't resolve is pushed to a group chat message for the siblings to settle.
needs: Calendar access (Google or ICS) for each sibling
Group messaging channel such as Telegram or email
Anthropic API key
Written consent and input from every family member including the parent

Qualitative interview study of AI for care coordination in cognitive decline. It asks whether agents could help coordinate, but no multi-agent sibling rota is built.

CareCommons: free iPhone app for siblings sharing parent care; shared task board, care log, schedules; nudges to redistribute when tasks pile on one person. No negotiation, no parent agent, no ledger of drives/money, AI not mentioned.
Caring Village: established care-circle app (siblings coordinate care, shared calendar, tasks); human-driven, no fairness ledger or agents. Seen in search results only.
Kinship: multi-agent eldercare system (agent for older adult, agent for daughter caregiver) with human-approved proposals. Opened; no siblings, fairness or negotiation.

dossier.title: Overnight battery drain traced by controlled experiments
dossier.text: Runs controlled overnight experiments on an Android phone over adb, toggling radios, sync and app standby buckets while logging battery stats, then ranks which setting explains the unexplained drain.
dossier.pitch: For anyone whose phone loses 15 percent overnight and who is tired of forum folklore. An experiment loop plans a test matrix, runs one night per condition, and reports effect sizes with confidence. Nobody does this because a single night is noisy and the bookkeeping across nights is tedious, and the loop does the bookkeeping.
dossier.demo_60s: Time-lapse of a phone on a USB cable, then a screen with a table of eight overnight conditions and measured percent drain per hour for each. The final slide is a ranked bar chart with intervals showing that one sync setting and background location explain most of the drain, followed by a one-paragraph written finding and the exact adb commands to reproduce it.
needs: Android phone with USB debugging enabled
USB cable and a Windows 11 PC with Python and adb
a few nights of runtime
optional: USB power meter

closest.what: Nothing Community thread 'Investigating Nothing OS CPU Idle Behavior - Wake Locks & Background Services'. I could not read the body, so I don't know whether adb experiments or multi-night runs were involved. Likely an anecdote, not a controlled loop.

A non-AI framework that automates repeated Android battery experiments from JSON configs, with a batterystats plugin and run hooks. It covers the experiment-loop and bookkeeping half of the concept, but has no overnight scope, no setting-toggle ranking and no AI.

Python tool that parses an adb bugreport into top wakelock holders, per-app CPU and network, and alarm wakeups. The repo lists a battery_drain_test.sh, but the README does not describe it. It only attributes drain from a single capture, has no controlled toggling, and the page does not mention AI.

Android Runner: automates repeated measurement experiments on Android devices over adb with profiler plugins. Closest on experiment orchestration and bookkeeping. The page I opened does not confirm settings toggling or statistics, and it targets app energy research rather than a user's unexplained overnight drain.

ARENA: Android Studio plugin that resets battery stats per iteration and runs R statistics (Kruskal-Wallis, ANOVA). Covers repeated runs plus analysis. Hardware-measurement oriented, and I did not confirm automatic settings toggling. Seen in search results only, not opened.

Battery Historian: analyzes bugreports (wakelocks, timelines) and offers A/B comparison of two bugreports. Archived Dec 2022. It does not run experiments, so the human does the bookkeeping across nights.

dossier.title: Release notes versus firmware binaries across five years
dossier.text: Downloads every public firmware release of a consumer gadget line, unpacks and diffs them, and tabulates what silently changed in endpoints, permissions, ciphers and features against what the release notes claimed.
dossier.pitch: For privacy researchers, consumer journalists and owners deciding whether to update. It treats a product's update history as a dataset and asks what the vendor changed that it never said. Nobody does this at scale because unpacking, diffing and reading dozens of images per product is weeks of grind.
dossier.demo_60s: Pick an e-reader or camera line from a list. Progress shows 40 firmware files fetched and unpacked, then a timeline with release notes on top and measured changes below. Red markers show an added telemetry hostname in 2022, a removed local-API feature, and a weakened TLS setting, each clickable to the diff evidence.
needs: public firmware download URLs for one product line
7-Zip or Python archive libraries
Windows 11 PC with Python and Node
disk space of a few GB
internet

closest.what: Fetches old and new binaries, runs Ghidriff diffs, then an LLM pipeline (OpenAI, Claude or Ollama) writes severity-rated reports. This is AI-assisted binary diffing, but for security patch diffing. It has no release-notes comparison, no multi-year corpus and no consumer-gadget focus.

Pre-alpha multi-agent LLM pipeline. Ghidra decompiles two binaries, an analyzer classes each change as bugfix, feature, refactor or security tweak, and a critic and clusterer follow. The only example is a cJSON library version pair, and it does not check release notes.
2025 paper on LLM binary diff summarization. It adds natural-language summaries to binary diffs, with no release-notes comparison and no product-history dataset.

Public, continuously updated Apple IPSW firmware diffs across many iOS/iPadOS/macOS releases (via the ipsw tool). It is the same method (unpack and diff every release) but is aimed at security researchers, covers Apple only, and does no comparison against release notes or any privacy tabulation.

AI-written reports built on ipsw diffing of iOS releases. It uses AI to describe what changed between firmware builds, but is vulnerability-oriented, covers a single platform, and does not compare against release-note claims.

AutoFirm (seen in search results, not opened): large-scale analysis of 6,901 IoT firmware images that tracks reused and outdated libraries across versions. It is a longitudinal firmware dataset study but does not check release-note fidelity.

dossier.title: Cloud shutdown drill for every gadget at home
dossier.text: Sinkholes each household gadget's vendor domains one at a time from a laptop hotspot, tests which features survive, and produces a ranked map of what bricks if the cloud disappears.
dossier.pitch: For smart-home owners and repair advocates who worry about the next vendor shutdown. A drill harness plans which domains to block, drives each device's features through its app or local interface, and records what keeps working offline. Nobody has made this systematic because testing one device takes an afternoon and finding the critical domain is guesswork.
dossier.demo_60s: A laptop hotspot runs with three devices attached, a smart plug, a TV and an e-reader. The harness blocks one domain at a time while a live grid fills in with green for works, amber for degraded, red for bricked. It ends with a one-page cloud-dependence report showing that the plug dies when one domain goes, while the TV only loses ads and voice search.
needs: Windows 11 PC with Wi-Fi that supports mobile hotspot
a DNS sinkhole such as dnsmasq or a Python resolver
two to ten owned consumer devices
their companion apps on a phone
packet capture tool

closest.what: Manual test of a hub's offline capabilities per device/feature. Human-run, one platform, no domain sinkholing, no ranking, no AI.
Anecdotal article: a person blocked internet on all smart devices and reported what still worked. Blanket block, manual, no per-domain drill, no AI.
Tester cut internet and checked which Matter devices worked offline via Apple Home. Manual, per-device observations, no AI.

IoTrimmer (Mandalari, Kolcun, Haddadi, Dubois, Choffnes): research framework that tests which destinations a consumer IoT device contacts and blocks those not needed for functionality. Same mechanism (per-destination blocking, check function survives) but aimed at privacy, not a ranked 'what bricks' map; no public code found.

Home Assistant IoT classes (cloud polling/push vs local polling/push): established practice that classifies each integration by cloud dependency. A declared label per integration, not an empirically tested drill.
DIY practice guide: block device internet at router/firewall, log contacted servers, check what still works. Manual, per device, no harness.
